turns.response_html:
That "spinning in place" while the engine screams and heats up is incredibly common. It’s a phenomenon called cavitation — essentially, the blades spin so fast they create a pocket of air or a vacuum around themselves, and the thick food gets stuck like a wall above them, completely out of reach.

When you’re blending dense, starchy things like soaked and boiled beans (which are notorious for soaking up moisture and turning into paste), the blender relies entirely on a fluid vortex to pull the top layer down into the blades.

Here is how to structure your blender pitcher next time to prevent cavitation and keep the motor cool:

The Golden Order of Loading

The absolute rule of thumb for a standard blender is liquids first, solids last.

  • Bottom (Nearest the Blades): Liquids, oils, yogurt, or water. This ensures the blades immediately have something fluid to catch and spin, creating a vortex right away.
  • Middle: Soft items, powders, and cooked ingredients (like your beans).
  • Top: Hard, frozen, or heavy items. Their weight helps push the lower ingredients down into the vortex.

3 Quick Fixes for Thick Blends

If you notice the blender spinning freely but nothing is moving, stop it immediately. To get it moving without just diluting your recipe with endless water, try this:

  1. Use the Tamper (If you have one): If your blender came with a plastic bat/plunger that fits through the lid, use it while blending. It is physically designed to smash those air pockets and push the beans back into the blades safely without hitting the spinning mechanism.
  2. Pulse, Don't Shake: Instead of turning it on high and letting it run, use the Pulse button. Pulsing forces the motor to start and stop, which allows gravity to drop the thick paste back down onto the blades between bursts.
  3. The "Vortex Test": If you see a small funnel form in the center of the food, it's working. If the top surface is completely still while the bottom is spinning, you need to add liquid (broth, water, or oil) 2 to 3 tablespoons at a time until that funnel appears.

Beans are basically pure starch, so they act like a sponge. Even fully cooked, soft beans need a surprising amount of liquid lubrication to keep from turning into mortar.

turns.prompt_text: So essentially I need to pour a bunch of water in the blender and start it blending and then slowly pour actual food in Because the vortex is necessary And then I can really boil the water out or crush it out later
turns.response_html:
Not quite! You actually don't want to start with a blender full of spinning water and drop items into it. That's a surefire way to get a face full of hot bean water or cause the liquid to splash violently against the lid.

Instead, you keep everything inside the pitcher from the start—you just change the layering and the ratio.

Here is how the vortex actually works in practice:

The "Static Layer" Method

You don't need the blades spinning before the food goes in. You just need the liquid sitting at the bottom so it's the very first thing the blades touch when you turn the machine on.

  1. Pour the liquid in first (just enough to cover the blades completely, usually about $1/2$ to 1 cup depending on your blender).
  2. Pile your beans on top of the liquid while the machine is completely off.
  3. Put the lid on, start on LOW, and let the blades throw that bottom liquid up into the beans.

As the liquid mixes with the bottom layer of beans, it turns them into a thin puree. That puree then acts as the "liquid" that pulls the next layer of beans down. It builds its own momentum.

Why "Boiling it Out Later" is a Trap

Trying to blend with way too much water and cooking it off later is a massive headache. Because beans are so high in starch, if you add too much water, you end up with a massive pot of watery bean soup. Boiling that down to a thick paste or dip takes a long time, requires constant stirring so the bottom doesn't burn, and can drastically alter the flavor.

Instead of fixing it later, the goal is to find the minimum effective amount of liquid from the start.

The 3-Tablespoon Rule: If your blender stalls, don't dump a cup of water in. Add just 2 to 3 tablespoons of liquid, pulse it a few times to let it sink to the bottom, and try again. Repeat only until the vortex forms.

What are you ultimately trying to make with the beans? (Like a smooth hummus, a black bean dip, or a base for a soup?) Knowing the end goal changes exactly how much liquid you can afford to sneak in.
